title: The universe's rules likely yield a unique causal network

fields.label: Label
fields.value: The universe's rules likely yield a unique causal network

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Although the universe has no global clock and its rules may be applicable in arbitrary order, its actual rules most likely have the property of always yielding the same causal network, and so a unique perceived history.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: it still tends to be my suspicion that there is not—and that in fact the particular rules followed by the universe do in the end have the property that they always yield the same causal network.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 9, “Fundamental Physics”; section “Evolution of Networks” (from p. 508), p. 508. Scope: the fundamental update rules of the universe

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch09-18: needs-new-data, resolvability 0.31

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Causal invariance is decidable for some proposed rules, but the claim concerns the unknown rule of the universe. Existing observations lack the resolution and model specificity needed to identify that property.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Specify candidate fundamental rewrite rules and compare predictions generated under different update orders with observations of spacetime and particle physics. Evidence for order-dependent observable histories would refute causal invariance; a uniquely successful invariant rule would support it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Current data do not reveal microscopic update order.

The actual rule is unknown.

Many causally invariant rules may be observationally equivalent.

fields.value:

discriminating power: 0.4

analysis feasibility: 0.2

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Causal invariance is a sharp property of a rewrite system, and it is checkable for any fully specified rule. The claim applies it to the universe's actual rules, which are not in hand, and the single history we observe does not distinguish that mechanism from standard relativistic spacetime. Settling it requires either those rules or a new signature of non-invariance.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Once a candidate rule for the universe is fixed, test whether every allowed update order produces one causal network. A rule that reproduces observed physics and is causally invariant would support the claim; a rule that reproduces physics only along some orders, with observable branching, would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A unique perceived history is also predicted by ordinary continuum spacetime, so it does not isolate causal invariance.

The actual update rule is unknown, so the property cannot be evaluated on the object the claim is about.
